In setup-pipeline, notebooks 02 (dimension validation), 03, 04, and 05 run in parallel after 01. Notebooks 06, 07, and 08 run in parallel after 03; 09 waits for 03 to 06. Each notebook runs its own stages concurrently and passes outputs to later notebooks as gen__* tables in the Silver staging schema.

Setup 10 checks invariants and publishes Silver atomically once 02 to 09 succeed. Setup 11 builds Gold inside ml-required, alongside model training, because both read only Silver.

items.title: Required tokens
items.text:
Token Meaning LAKEHOUSE_NAME Target Lakehouse display name SILVER_DB Silver schema, normally ag GOLD_DB Gold schema, normally au STORE_TYPE Dictionary/profile START_DATE Derived or explicit historical start END_DATE Derived or explicit historical end STORE_COUNT Number of stores SEED Deterministic seed DICTIONARY_REF Git ref used for dictionary content

stream-events is rendered with the setup notebooks but is staged separately and is not part of the ordered setup pipeline.

items.title: deploy
items.text:
Common flags:

  • --env <name>
  • --skip-terraform
  • --dry-run
  • --yes
  • --recreate
  • --resume

--recreate and --skip-terraform cannot be combined. A non-dry-run deploy loads the environment, validates the current Azure CLI tenant where applicable, detects an existing workspace for interactive reset, executes the deployment plan, and deploys the task flow where selected.

setup-pipeline includes only setup notebooks 01 through 11. For profiles that publish Reporting, deploy then runs ml-required with terminal polling. Its six producers (demand forecast, customer segmentation, churn, stockout, market-basket mining, and promotion/elasticity analysis) feed 15-validate-required-ml-contract; only exact-run success allows a second publication phase to stage the semantic model and report. full-demo runs ml-optional and ml-experimental afterward.

After those pipelines, deployment synchronizes Lakehouse SQL endpoint metadata. This makes newly written tables visible to SQL and Power BI clients. The step is optional because readiness independently fails closed when a required table is unavailable.

The deployment artifact build also consumes the render manifest and rewrites the staged Power BI report date filters to the month containing end_date. The committed Power BI Project (PBIP) remains an authoring template, while each deployed report opens on the latest month generated by that setup, including custom months or explicit date ranges.

Terraform apply consumes the saved, validated plan. --yes pre-confirms Terraform apply but does not skip the destructive-change guard, required pipeline gates or live tenant/capacity preflight. Full-demo's capability preflight needs no prompt when the required tenant switches and capacity are valid. Disabled settings and invalid capacity fail before Fabric changes, with instructions for correcting the problem. --skip-terraform rejects missing, placeholder, incomplete, or wrong-workspace Terraform outputs before publication. --recreate polls for workspace-name release for up to 180 seconds between destroy and apply.

--resume reuses only the contiguous succeeded prefix of an incomplete journal with matching targets and source/config/plan fingerprint. Pending apply or publication consumers refresh their plan or staged inputs before retry. Legacy journals missing the new compatibility fields are not resumable. The prior journal is archived before a different resumed/new run becomes latest. See the deployment specification for compatibility and recreate restrictions.

For standard and full-demo, deployment finishes with a read-only live readiness verification. It never triggers an additional pipeline. Required failed/unknown evidence fails deployment, while optional failed/unknown evidence records a degraded run.

For full-demo, deployment automatically checks for the stable ontology. When it is absent, the orchestrator runs the deployed 30-create-ontology notebook, waits for the item, publishes both Data Agents, deploys all selected task-flow references, and verifies the graph after persistence. The retail-setup post-ontology --env <name> command remains as an idempotent repair path. Optional stream freshness can leave either path DEGRADED without failing required ontology/task-flow publication.

items.title: verify
items.text:
retail-setup verify --env <name> queries profile-selected live items, definitions, task flow, KQL objects, schedules, pipeline jobs, and freshness signals. It writes deploy/.generated/<env>/readiness-report.json atomically and returns 0 for success, 1 for required failure/unknown, 2 for usage, or 3 for optional degradation.

The default is read-only. --run-pipeline is the only mutating verifier flag; it explicitly starts and waits for the profile-required post-publish pipeline. It is rejected for profiles without that pipeline and does not start streaming or other workloads.

items.title: Output behavior
items.text: CLI output is linear plain text with ASCII separators. Required command failures propagate from the plan. Task-flow and pipeline gate/failure behavior is documented in the deployment specification and operations runbook.

items.title: Evidence
items.text:
• utility/src/retail_setup/cli/main.py
  • utility/src/retail_setup/notebooks/inject.py
  • utility/src/retail_setup/config/generation.py
  • utility/tests/test_cli_configure.py

items.title: Runtime
items.text:
stream-events.ipynb is rendered from utility/notebooks/templates/driver-05-stream.py. It is an optional, long-running Fabric Spark Structured Streaming driver.

Supported sinks:

  • eventhouse: direct typed writes through the Spark Kusto connector;
  • delta: development/validation landing table.

The current path does not require Kafka, Event Hubs, or a Fabric Eventstream.

Before emitting events, the driver requires readable, nonempty Silver dim_stores, dim_customers, dim_products, dim_distribution_centers, and dim_trucks. Product/store attribute reads provide prices and tax data. Missing/empty dimensions or failed attribute reads stop startup rather than substituting arbitrary ID ranges or synthetic attribute frames. Complete historical setup before starting the stream.

items.title: Envelope
items.text:
Every event contains:

  • event_type
  • trace_id
  • ingest_timestamp
  • schema_version
  • source
  • correlation_id
  • partition_key
  • session_id
  • parent_event_id

Payload fields are event-specific and mapped by EVENT_PAYLOADS.

items.title: Business event types
items.text:
1. receipt_created
  2. receipt_line_added
  3. payment_processed
  4. inventory_updated
  5. stockout_detected
  6. reorder_triggered
  7. customer_entered
  8. customer_zone_changed
  9. ble_ping_detected
  10. truck_arrived
  11. truck_departed
  12. store_opened
  13. store_closed
  14. ad_impression
  15. promotion_applied
  16. online_order_created
  17. online_order_picked
  18. online_order_shipped

KQL defines an additional unknown_event catch-all table. It is not a nineteenth generated business event. The current notebook rejects unmapped event types before committing the micro-batch checkpoint. The catch-all is an operational queued-ingestion boundary, not an active direct-writer DLQ. Here DLQ means dead-letter queue: a place to preserve messages that could not be processed.

items.title: Eventhouse writes
items.text:
For each micro-batch, the notebook:

  1. Persists the batch.
  2. Finds present mapped event types.
  3. Resolves one notebook runtime token.
  4. Maps JSON to typed envelope/payload columns.
  5. Writes event types concurrently to their same-named KQL tables.
  6. Uses FailIfNotExist.
  7. Sets flushImmediately=true.
  8. Unpersists the batch.

If kusto_uri is blank, the notebook resolves the KQL database queryServiceUri by display name in the current workspace.

items.title: Trigger and checkpoint behavior
items.text:
• Eventhouse uses a 10-second processing trigger for an unbounded run.
  • Bounded runs use a 2-second processing trigger.
  • Checkpoints are sink-specific under Files/setup/stream/checkpoint/<sink>.
  • A logical stream ID is stored under the checkpoint root. Notebook restarts reuse it; deleting the checkpoint root creates a new event-ID namespace.

items.title: Duplicate and failure behavior
items.text:
• Generated business IDs and trace_id include the persisted stream ID.
  • Eventhouse writes use the connector's transactional mode, deterministic request IDs, duplicate-blob protection, and matching ingest-by/check tags for each stream, event type, and Spark micro-batch.
  • Unmapped event types and any required table-write failure raise from foreachBatch, so Spark does not commit that batch's checkpoint.
  • Silver transforms remove exact duplicate candidates, reject conflicting rows with the same identity, and use Delta MERGE before advancing watermarks.
  • Gold tables are rebuilt with overwrite semantics from duplicate-safe Silver inputs, so reruns do not accumulate aggregate rows.

These controls make expected retries idempotent and are covered by injected failure/replay contracts. tests/test_streaming_dedup_contract.py executes the actual foreachBatch sink function with mocked connector operations, including partial table-write, unmapped-event, and credential failures. These tests do not establish live Spark/Kusto transactional behavior. The readiness adapter checks live ingestion and checkpoint tags. The remaining IMP-013 evidence includes a recent bounded run of the intentionally manual stream and live execution of the bounded receipt/inventory/sales reconciliation query.

items.title: Cross-layer ownership
items.text:
The exact KQL table shape is in 01-create-tables.kql. JSON ingestion mappings in 02-create-ingestion-mappings.kql support queued raw-JSON ingestion but are not used by the direct typed live path.

Silver mappings are separately implemented in fabric/lakehouse/03-streaming-to-silver.ipynb. Their current divergence from the historical contract is documented in Fabric analytics.

contracts/retail-demo.json declares one stable path ID per emitted event and one derived attribution path. It stores keys, UTC event-time semantics, targets, terminals, and named exceptions, but never copies physical field or type inventories. python scripts/check_data_contracts.py derives those inventories from the driver, KQL, schemas.py, notebooks, and active TMDL.

items.title: Truck lifecycle
items.text:
truck_arrived and truck_departed share truck_id, dc_id, store_id, and shipment_id. The departure payload and envelope timestamp are later than the arrival timestamp. Normal dwell is a deterministic 30-75 minutes; every fifth eligible logistics value takes the deterministic 120-minute late path, above the 90-minute rule threshold.

Silver joins the two event tables on all four lifecycle keys and writes one completed fact_truck_moves row. Eventhouse and Gold expose dwell in minutes with STORE_<id> / DC_<id> site labels.

tests/test_truck_dwell_contract.py verifies the generator, rendered stream notebook, KQL table/function contract, Silver join, Gold aggregation, queryset, dashboard template, and 90-minute rule. A live Fabric smoke run remains the deployment verification gate.

items.title: Marketing attribution
items.text:
Attributed store and online scenarios emit two ad_impression touches and one purchase journey without introducing another event type. The existing envelope correlation_id carries attribution_journey_id through impressions, receipt/order creation, promotion, payment, and online status events.

The contract is deterministic last-touch within an inclusive seven-day window, ordered by touch timestamp and impression ID. Silver writes one fact_marketing_attribution row after purchase, promotion, and approved payment reconcile; attributed rows additionally require a valid selected touch, while purchases without a journey are marked UNATTRIBUTED_NO_JOURNEY.

Money remains integer cents:

gross_subtotal_cents - discount_cents = net_subtotal_cents
net_subtotal_cents + tax_cents = total_cents
approved payment_cents = total_cents
attributed_revenue_cents = net_subtotal_cents

Eventhouse exposes reconciliation diagnostics through fn_marketing_attribution(). Consumer-facing fn_attribution() and fn_attribution_window() return only reconciled ATTRIBUTED purchases after future and out-of-window touches are removed and the latest valid touch is selected. fn_campaign_performance() uses that reconciled set. Gold publishes campaign_performance_daily, and the Direct Lake model exposes both the audit fact and campaign KPIs. Contract tests cover batch determinism, live payload/KQL mappings, Silver/Gold wiring, semantic measures, and all cent equations. A live Fabric smoke run remains the deployment verification gate.

items.title: Contract evidence and live boundary
items.text:
Eight fixture scenarios cover all 18 emitted types plus nullable and unknown-event variants. The parameterized matrix validates the nine-field envelope, KQL DDL/mappings, UTC values, business/dedupe keys, Silver/Gold routes, and either an active semantic terminal or the named streaming-only exception.

Repository acceptance for IMP-005 is complete. A live Fabric staging run through Eventhouse, the optional Silver/Gold projection, and Direct Lake remains required external evidence. The static check does not prove tenant-level execution.

items.title: Guides
items.text:
Choose a guide for the task at hand. You can start with setup, a workspace tour, presentation steps, or operations; there is no required reading order.

If Fabric terminology is new to you, keep the plain-language glossary open while you work.

For exact schemas, interfaces, or acceptance criteria, see Design documentation.

items.title: CIO walkthrough
items.text:
Use this walkthrough to show a CIO and their leadership team how Power BI, chat, and two operations agents use the same Fabric retail data. Allow about 15 minutes for the main path or 25 minutes with the additional questions. Start with the report, ask questions in chat, then review a replenishment proposal and a retention campaign draft.

Rehearse against the selected environment and read its readiness report first. This guide is not a live acceptance record. Replay uses synthetic fixtures, and approvals create local demo state, not production orders or campaigns. The app attempts to send action telemetry to Eventhouse, but delivery is not guaranteed.

items.title: Before we start: what's deployed, and why it's useful
items.text:
The data platform is organized in one Fabric workspace. The local app, operator browser, identity provider, and optional router are additional trust and cost boundaries. Four data capabilities share that Fabric foundation:

Layer Fabric component Questions it supports Historical analytics Semantic model (Direct Lake over the Gold Lakehouse) Totals, rankings, and trends Relationships Ontology (graph of business entities) Connections between named entities Real-time Eventhouse (KQL) and streaming Recent sales and operational events Prediction ML models (Gold tables) Forecasts, risk estimates, and pricing recommendations

The same Gold tables feed the report, agents, and models. Eventhouse holds live sales events and any agent telemetry that the app successfully delivers.

Use the semantic model for aggregates such as net sales by region. Use the ontology to connect a named synthetic customer's profile with their segment and churn prediction. Broad aggregations and deep scans generally belong on the semantic model; verify that the selected graph lookup works before the presentation.

See Agentic application for the architecture and service boundaries.

items.title: The interface: what's on screen
items.text:
The Dashboard page places the Power BI report beside the Ask-your-data chat, using about 70% and 30% of the space, respectively. The orchestrator routes each question without asking the presenter to choose a data source.

The Agent Operations page shows an approval funnel from the Eventhouse agent_actions table and refreshes every few seconds.

Expand how I reached this below an answer to inspect the source, router model, call, and result preview. Operations-agent traces include the DAX. Fabric MCP services do not return their generated query text.

items.title: The walkthrough: see it, ask it, act on it
Act 1: See it (Power BI, ~3 min)
items.text:
Open Dashboard, let the report load, then expand these visuals:

  1. Executive sales and margin: show net sales, gross margin %, and channel mix.
  2. Inventory and stockout risk: identify stores to revisit in the replenishment example.
  3. Customer and churn: identify segments to revisit in the retention example.

Suggested narration: "The report shows the selected period's sales and risk signals. Now let's ask a question about the same data."

items.title: Act 2: Ask it (chat, ~5 min)
items.text:
Ask these in order. Expand how I reached this after each answer to show which source answered and why.

# Ask this Source the agent uses Why this question 1 "What were total net sales and gross margin company-wide?" Semantic model Compare chat with the report for the same period 2 "What are the top products by revenue last month, and each one's gross margin %?" Semantic model Check a ranked list with a second measure 3 Ask for the segment and churn probability of an observed loyalty card Ontology Use an authorized synthetic key present in this environment 4 "How many customers are predicted to churn, and what is their total lifetime value?" Semantic model over the ML churn table Inspect model estimates alongside historical value 5 "What were the top-selling products in the last 15 minutes?" Live-sales shortcut; inspect the trace Check freshness, time window, and whether the result is at product or store grain

Suggested narration: "The trace shows which source answered and why. We can compare its result with the report or underlying data."

items.title: Act 3: Act on it (operations agents, ~6 min)
items.text:
Ask a question that requests a decision. The orchestrator hands it to an operations agent, which reads the deployed synthetic data, applies business rules, and drafts a proposal for review.

For Inventory & Replenishment, ask: "What products are at risk of stockout, and what should we do about it?"

Inspect the exposure count and assumptions from the actual response, then the trace: stockout risk → covering reorders → product prices → coverage rule. Review the recommendation card's evidence before approving one local draft. Do not repeat counts or dollar amounts from an older workspace.

For Customer Retention, ask: "Customer churn is rising. What can we do to retain customers?"

Use the current response's cohort count and modeled lifetime-value estimate; these are synthetic risk indicators, not guaranteed recoverable revenue. The trace should show the ML churn read, the join to customer_segments for lifetime value (LTV), cohort selection, and cross-sell suggestions from the market-basket model. Review the draft campaign's Approve and Dismiss controls.

Suggested narration: "Each agent proposes a specific action and shows its evidence. Approval records a local decision; it does not execute an order or campaign."

items.title: Validate it: close the loop
items.text:
Inspect whether each expected draft/decision reached agent_actions. The app attempts Eventhouse logging asynchronously and can lose events without failing the chat or approval. Local approval success is not proof of telemetry delivery or an immutable audit record.

Switch to Agent Operations after Act 3. Check the proposed and approved action counts, estimated replenishment value, and churn LTV associated with the proposals. Confirm actual delivery time rather than promising a fixed latency. Query the ingested events with KQL:

agent_actions
| summarize actions = count(), ltv_at_risk = sum(ltv_at_risk) by agent, action_status
| order by agent asc

These events can support an operations dashboard. Their presence does not establish a complete or immutable approval audit.

items.title: Appendix: deep-cut questions (if time allows)
items.text:
Use these questions to explore combined metrics and model outputs:

  • "What is the total modeled lifetime value of high-churn-risk customers?" Inspect the estimate's limitations before reviewing a local campaign draft.
  • "For products at high stockout risk, estimate the at-risk daily sales." Review the assumptions before approving a local reorder draft.
  • "For each underperforming store, list its top stockout risk, churn-risk customers, and recommended cross-sell." Present this composed action list as a proposal, not a current capability.

items.title: Appendix: pre-flight checklist
items.text:
• Fabric capacity is Active; check the environment's actual pause policy.
  • Local app on loopback; signed in as an operator with only necessary permissions.
  • Streaming notebook running so "last 15 minutes" returns fresh data.
  • Preserve prior telemetry and proposal evidence; do not clear shared state merely to make presentation counters start at zero.
  • Run the Inventory and Retention questions once before presenting; initial DAX reads can take a few seconds.

items.title: Report-to-chat handoff and fallback
items.text:
Use Executive, Sales, Supply Chain, store/product drillthrough, Omnichannel, and Operations/Marketing pages to identify the period, store, product, or cohort before asking. A report slicer is not automatically chat context: include the observed key/name and period in the question. Do not invent a loyalty-card field on report pages that do not expose one.

Prefer named-entity, single-relationship graph questions. Break broad multi-hop/event traversals into smaller questions or use semantic-model aggregation. Inspect source, grain, window, fallback, and empty/error results; the current live-sales shortcut has a fixed store-sales window and does not prove arbitrary product/window answers. See routing.

If a service stalls, show a previously validated report view or explicitly labeled replay, and retain the failure for follow-up. Use the evaluation question bank to explore broader prompts; do not reuse old results as current evidence. Pricing, logistics, merchandising, and composed per-store actions remain proposals.

items.title: Presenter demo script
items.text:
Audience: Retail operations, analytics, and technology stakeholders Duration: 15-20 minutes Data: Synthetic

For a browser-first tour of the deployed workspace, use the deployed solution walkthrough.

For a standalone 5-7 minute persona walkthrough, use the presenter journeys for retail operations, merchandising, or executive/analytics audiences.

items.title: Before the audience arrives
items.text:
1. Complete the getting-started guide.
  2. Confirm the required KQL tables and ag/au Lakehouse tables exist.
  3. Open the Eventhouse query editor, Power BI report, and the streaming notebook.
  4. Check whether the dashboard, ontology, agents, and ML outputs are ready. Skip any feature whose source, permission, or capability checks have failed.
  5. Keep the operations guide open for recovery.

items.title: 1. Frame the architecture
items.text:
Open the architecture overview.

Talk track:

  • Setup notebooks create repeatable historical data. Silver is the cleaned, detailed layer; Gold is the business-ready summary layer.
  • stream-events.ipynb writes eighteen live event types directly to Eventhouse.
  • KQL (Kusto Query Language) answers recent event questions; Lakehouse stores durable history and summaries.
  • Power BI uses Direct Lake, which reads Lakehouse data without importing a second copy.
  • Optional ontology and agents add business context after their capability and binding checks pass.

items.title: 2. Start live data
items.text:
In stream-events.ipynb, select the Eventhouse sink and run a bounded stream. Show a recent row:

receipt_created
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(10m)
| take 10

Then show live sales aggregation:

mv_store_sales_minute
| where ts > ago(10m)
| summarize sales = sum(total_sales) by store_id
| order by sales desc

Suggested talk track:

Each generated business event says what happened and when. A unique trace identifier connects related receipt, line-item, promotion, and payment events, so we can follow one synthetic transaction across the process. The payload also identifies the store or order used to keep related events together. Eventhouse records when it received each event, which lets us prove that the optional stream is currently active.

items.title: 3. Ask operational questions
items.text:
Choose a supported path from the presenter journeys, or use checked-in queryset tabs for:

  • Recent sales and top products.
  • Inventory movements and stockout detections.
  • Omnichannel order creation and fulfillment events.
  • Store presence and zone dwell.

Be precise: recent stockout detections are not the same as unresolved current stockout state. Truck dwell is implemented and covered by cross-layer contract tests, but present it only after a bounded live run produces recent fn_truck_sla() rows in the selected workspace.

items.title: 4. Show durable history
items.text:
Run or show the last successful streaming-to-Silver/Gold pipeline. In the Lakehouse:

  • inspect ag.fact_receipts or another mapped fact;
  • inspect a Gold aggregate such as au.sales_minute_store;
  • show run or watermark evidence rather than relying on visual freshness alone.

items.title: 5. Show Power BI
items.text:
Open the Power BI Project (PBIP) report and demonstrate historical and operational pages backed by the Direct Lake model. Use explicit measures and current data periods.

Deployment saves each date filter to the month containing the configured history end date. State that month before showing a number. If the report was rerendered with a different history window, its default month changes with the data.

If required ML tables have not been generated and validated, do not present predictive pages as supported output.

items.title: 6. Close with actions and roadmap
items.text:
If a pricing approval or alert scenario has been validated, show it as an optional action. In full-demo, you can also open the retail-approvals Fabric App to show a different reviewer recording an append-only decision on a replenishment proposal; the app does not place orders. RTI dashboards and Activator rules are checked in as design and reference material, not deployed items. Otherwise, describe the action story from the owning backlog:

  • RTI dashboards and Activator
  • Closed-loop pricing

items.title: Do not overclaim
items.text:
Keep these qualifications in the presentation:

  • Truck dwell behavior is owned by the event contract; do not present it as live-validated until a Fabric smoke run has been recorded.
  • Marketing attribution and return on ad spend (ROAS) are implemented and contract-tested. State the seven-day last-touch rule and selected data period before presenting a result.
  • Required ML publication has been exercised live and remains fail-closed. Still check the current readiness report before presenting predictions, because model evidence is time-bounded.

items.title: Deployed walkthrough: analytics and AI
items.text:
Allow 10-15 minutes to show retail and analytics teams the ontology, Data Agents, and Power BI report over synthetic data. Start with the walkthrough overview.

Optional surfaces

Ontology and Data Agents require valid source bindings, permissions, and capability support. Skip a feature that has not passed its preflight checks.

items.title: 1. Show business context in the ontology
items.text:
An ontology is a business map that connects concepts such as Store, Product, Customer, and Receipt to the underlying data. Show this section only after deployment confirmed that the ontology exists and points to the intended Lakehouse and Eventhouse sources.

  1. Open the Ontologies folder.
  2. Open RetailOntology_AutoGen.
  3. Select the Store entity type in Explorer.
  4. Select Relationship to show only the entities connected to Store.

The Relationship view shows Store connected to Geography, Receipt, Promotion, and the machine-learning StockoutRisk entity.

The ontology maps business concepts to existing Lakehouse and Eventhouse data. It does not replace the physical schema or copy the source data.

items.title: 2. Test a grounded data-agent answer
items.text:
If the semantic-model agent passed its source and permission checks:

  1. Open the Agents folder.
  2. Open retail-semantic-model-agent.
  3. Select Test data agent.
  4. Ask for net sales and gross margin for a complete month, for example: "What were total net sales and gross margin % for September 2026? Name the measures used."

The data agent answers from the Net Sales and Gross Margin % measures and states the date range, so the result can be checked against the report.

The agent can use every table in retail_model, including the receipt-level fact tables. Ask about a complete month: the latest month is usually partial, so month-over-month and year-over-year figures for it look artificially low. If you compare with the report, set the report's date filter to the same month first. Check each generated answer against measures, query output, and source timestamps.

Skip an agent when it has no selected data sources, returns an error, or has not passed its capability and access checks. The ontology graph can still be shown independently when its bindings are valid.

items.title: 3. Close with the Power BI outcome
items.text:
1. Open the Reports folder.
  2. Open the retail_model report.
  3. Start on Executive Cockpit.
  4. Continue to Sales, Supply Chain Control Tower, Omnichannel Fulfillment, or Operations & Marketing when the audience wants more detail.

The Executive Cockpit combines omnichannel performance, store comparisons, ML risk signals, and an AI-generated narrative over the Direct Lake semantic model.

Direct Lake is the Power BI connection mode that reads Lakehouse tables directly without importing another data copy. The report opens on the latest month generated by this deployment, not a hard-coded month shared by every workspace.

State the selected data period before discussing a value. All values are synthetic, and an AI-generated narrative can contain inaccuracies. Use the underlying measures and source timestamps as evidence.

items.text:

The control tower combines inventory position, replenishment, and ML-predicted stockout risk.

Omnichannel Fulfillment combines store and online revenue with payment mix and demand forecasting.

items.title: 4. Optional full-demo extensions
items.text:
Show these surfaces only when deployment and readiness confirmed them in the target workspace.

Surface Where to find it What to say Connected operational twins retail-twins report in the Reports folder A separate report over the same governed data; it is not a page of retail_model. Post-Reporting extended ML ml-optional and ml-experimental pipelines Journey analysis (journey_patterns), delivery prediction (dwell_predictions), and experimental dynamic pricing (pricing_recommendations) run after Reporting and are not Reporting prerequisites. The merchandising portal shows item trends, in-stock rate, and days of cover over a synthetic sample catalog. The promotion studio models discount and break-even what-ifs. In replenishment approvals, a different reviewer records append-only decisions on proposals. The apps do not change prices, place orders, or execute transfers.

items.title: Fabric Apps gallery
items.text:
Each app opens from the Fabric Apps folder and requires Fabric sign-in. These screenshots use the apps' synthetic sample data.

Merchandising portalPromotion studioReplenishment approvals

Sales, gross profit, in-stock rate, and items needing attention, with a this-period versus previous-period trend and private saved views.

A discount and assumed uplift produce promoted price, revenue, gross profit, and the uplift needed to break even; saved scenarios compare side by side.

Pending proposals wait for a reviewer other than the submitter; decisions are append-only and a rejection needs a reason.

items.title: Connect from VS Code (MCP)
items.text:
The Data Agent and Ontology expose streamable-HTTP Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Call them from Copilot's agent-mode chat in VS Code to test questions before connecting them to the agentic application. Each call is a JSON-RPC POST authenticated with a Fabric bearer token.

The endpoint URLs follow these shapes (substitute your workspace, data-agent, and ontology-item GUIDs):

# Data Agent (semantic model)
https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/mcp/workspaces/{workspaceId}/dataagents/{dataAgentId}/agent

# Ontology (business graph)
https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/mcp/dataPlane/workspaces/{workspaceId}/items/{ontologyItemId}/ontologyEndpoint

1. Sign in to the tenant that owns the workspace:

az login

2. Obtain a Fabric token and copy the output. Tokens are valid for about 60-75 minutes:

az account get-access-token --resource https://api.fabric.microsoft.com --query accessToken -o tsv

3. Add .vscode/mcp.json (the .vscode/ folder is gitignored). VS Code prompts for the token once per session and passes it in the Authorization header:

{
  "inputs": [
    {
      "type": "promptString",
      "id": "fabric-token",
      "description": "Fabric bearer token (az account get-access-token --resource https://api.fabric.microsoft.com --query accessToken -o tsv)",
      "password": true
    }
  ],
  "servers": {
    "retail-data-agent": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/mcp/workspaces/{workspaceId}/dataagents/{dataAgentId}/agent",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:fabric-token}" }
    },
    "retail-ontology": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/mcp/dataPlane/workspaces/{workspaceId}/items/{ontologyItemId}/ontologyEndpoint",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:fabric-token}" }
    }
  }
}

4. Start the servers. Select Start above each server in .vscode/mcp.json, or run MCP: List Servers from the Command Palette. Paste the token, then open Copilot Chat in Agent mode and confirm both tools are enabled.

The Data Agent advertises one tool (DataAgent_<name>); the Ontology advertises list_ontology_entity_types and search_ontology. If calls return 401 because the token expired, repeat step 2, then use MCP: List Servers to restart the servers.

Which one to ask

Use the Data Agent for aggregates, rankings, and trends, such as the top 10 products by revenue last quarter. Use the Ontology for a named entity's related data, such as a loyalty member's segment and churn probability. Deep multi-hop scans can fail.

items.title: Deployed walkthrough: data platform
items.text:
Allow 10-15 minutes to show data engineering, analytics, and technology teams how Fabric loads, transforms, stores, and queries the synthetic retail data. Start with the walkthrough overview.

Representative screenshots

A deployed workspace can lag behind the repository. Use the current checked-in notebooks and schema contracts as the authority for exact behavior and field names.

items.title: 1. Show pipeline orchestration
items.text:
Open the Pipelines folder. Use the deployed pipelines to explain how notebooks are grouped into repeatable operations:

  • historical-data-load loads historical data into the Lakehouse.
  • streaming-data-load runs Silver transformation before Gold aggregation.
  • ml-required runs the six Reporting producers (including market-basket mining and promotion/elasticity analysis) and contract validator.
  • ml-optional and ml-experimental isolate full-demo extensions after Reporting.
Streaming transformsMachine learning

The streaming pipeline sequences 03-streaming-to-silver before 04-streaming-to-gold.

ml-required builds Gold with setup-11-build-gold, runs the six Reporting producers in parallel, and finishes with 15-validate-required-ml-contract.

ml-optional and ml-experimental are separate pipelines, so extended-model failures cannot block Reporting.

The pipeline canvas shows orchestration order. Use the Run history and activity output to confirm execution; a green dependency arrow only shows the intended order.

items.title: 2. Inspect a transformation notebook
items.text:
Open the Spark Notebooks folder, then open 03-streaming-to-silver.

The notebook moves new Eventhouse rows into Silver tables and uses a watermark to track the last processed event. Column names use snake_case.

Use the notebook header to explain the transform without scrolling through implementation details. Do not run the notebook until its Lakehouse binding and source tables have been verified.

The optional Eventhouse projection is prepared during deployment when streaming_shortcuts.enabled is true. For retail-demo, the deployment provisions OneLake mirroring with historical backfill and creates or verifies the shortcuts under Tables/cusn/ after KQL publication. The selected five-minute mirroring latency favors demo freshness but can produce smaller Parquet files; do not treat it as a production tuning recommendation.

items.title: 3. Inspect durable Lakehouse history
items.text:
1. Open retail_lakehouse.
  2. Expand Tables, then the ag schema.
  3. Select fact_receipts.

The Lakehouse explorer shows the Silver ag.fact_receipts table and a row preview from the generated historical dataset.

Point out:

  • ag contains cleaned, typed Silver dimensions and facts.
  • au contains business-ready Gold summaries used for analytics.
  • fact_receipts stores historical data with one row per receipt.
  • The preview demonstrates shape and content, not current operational freshness.

Use the authoritative historical data contract when explaining table ownership and columns.

items.title: 4. Inspect the Eventhouse hot path
items.text:
1. Open the retail_querysets KQL (Kusto Query Language) queryset.
  2. Confirm that retail_eventhouse appears in Explorer with the typed event tables.
  3. Select the q_receipts_minute_by_store tab. It reads the mv_store_sales_minute materialized view, which aggregates recent store sales.
  4. Select Run. If no stream has run in the last hour, widen lookback (for example to 7d) to show the most recent results.

The queryset reads per-minute store sales from the mv_store_sales_minute materialized view. This capture uses a seven-day lookback.

The materialized views are created by the numbered scripts in fabric/kql_database/ during deployment; the queryset holds the saved operational queries.

For live evidence, run a read-only query against a recent window:

receipt_created
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(10m)
| project ingest_timestamp, store_id, receipt_id, total
| order by ingest_timestamp desc
| take 10

Recent rows prove that Eventhouse ingestion is active. If the query is empty, show the schema and last known data timestamp, then follow the operations guide instead of claiming that the stream is live. Do not run the numbered deployment scripts during a presentation.

Open 03-streaming-to-silver The notebook identifies Eventhouse sources, Silver targets, and watermark-based processing. Use this browser tour to introduce a deployed workspace to retail, analytics, and technology teams. Allow 3-5 minutes for orientation or 15-25 minutes for the full walkthrough. All data is synthetic. The presenter demo provides a detailed talk track and limits on what to claim.

Representative screenshots

The screenshots show a representative deployment. Fabric navigation, generated values, item counts, and data timestamps can vary by deployment and run date. Validate freshness before presenting any value as current.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
1. Complete Getting started.
  2. Open the deployed Fabric workspace.
  3. Confirm that retail_lakehouse, retail_eventhouse, the KQL queryset, retail_model, the pipelines and notebooks, and any optional ontology or agent items you plan to show are available.

items.title: 1. Orient the audience in the workspace
items.text:
Open the workspace task flow and select the Retail Demo flow.

Task flow is a full-demo experience

The task flow is published only after the full-demo ontology step is complete. If the workspace uses core or standard, skip this step and open the workspace item list. You can still follow the historical, live, and Reporting paths described below.

The task flow maps ingestion, transformation, storage, the semantic model, ontology, ML, agents, case preparation, and Fabric Apps. Required ML feeds the Semantic Model; optional and experimental ML follows Reporting.

Explain the paths through the flow:

  • Load and transform deterministic retail history into the Lakehouse.
  • Send typed live events to Eventhouse and optionally project them into Lakehouse tables.
  • Make curated data available through the semantic model, Power BI, ontology, and Data Agents.

The task flow is a navigation aid. It does not prove that a notebook, pipeline, or stream completed successfully.
