items.title: Plain-language glossary
items.text: Look up unfamiliar terms from the guides, screenshots, and Fabric UI here. These definitions describe this demo, not every use of each term in Fabric.

items.title: Business and reporting terms
items.text: Term Plain-language meaning Business measure A reusable calculation, such as net sales or gross margin. Power BI and Data Agents use the same measure definitions to apply the same business rules. Dimension Descriptive data used to group or filter results. Examples include Store, Product, Customer, and Date. Fact A record of something that happened or changed, such as a receipt, payment, inventory movement, or online order. Grain What one row represents. A table with one row per receipt has a different grain from one with one row per product on a receipt. KPI Key performance indicator. A KPI is a measure used to monitor an outcome, such as sales, margin, stockout risk, or fulfillment time. ROAS Return on ad spend. It compares attributed sales with advertising cost. Attribution is an estimate, so ROAS should be presented with its time window and attribution rules. Semantic model The reusable Power BI data layer that defines tables, relationships, measures, and business-friendly names. It is often called a dataset in everyday Power BI conversation. Synthetic data Generated demonstration data that resembles business records but does not describe real customers, employees, stores, or transactions.

items.title: Microsoft Fabric terms
items.text: Term Plain-language meaning Capacity The Fabric computing resources that run notebooks, queries, pipelines, and reports. Larger or busier demos need more capacity. Activator Fabric's event-driven alerting and action service. The repository contains rule ideas, but the default deployment does not publish a complete Activator workflow. Data Agent A Fabric service that answers natural-language questions using approved data sources. Check each answer against its stated period, measures, and source data. Delta table A table stored in the Delta Lake format. Delta adds schema and transaction history to data files so that Spark and Fabric can update them safely. Direct Lake A Power BI connection mode that reads Fabric Lakehouse data directly from OneLake instead of copying it into a separate imported dataset. Eventhouse Fabric storage and query technology for high-volume, time-sensitive event data. This demo uses it for optional live retail events. Fabric workspace The shared Fabric area that contains the demo's Lakehouse, Eventhouse, notebooks, pipelines, reports, ontology, and other items. KQL Kusto Query Language, the query language used for Eventhouse data. KQL is designed for time-based events, logs, and operational analysis. KQL queryset A saved collection of KQL query tabs connected to an Eventhouse database. The demo deploys one queryset for repeatable operational questions. Lakehouse Fabric storage for data-lake files and tables, with Spark and SQL access. This demo uses it for historical and analytical tables. OneLake The organization-wide storage layer used by Microsoft Fabric. A Fabric Lakehouse stores its files and tables in OneLake. Ontology A map of business concepts, such as Store, Product, Customer, and Receipt, and their relationships to each other and the underlying data. Power BI Project (PBIP) The folder-based, source-control-friendly format used for the checked-in Power BI report and semantic model. Real-Time Intelligence (RTI) The Fabric workload for event-driven analysis. Eventhouse, KQL querysets, dashboards, and Activator are part of this area. Spark A distributed data-processing engine used by Fabric notebooks. The setup and machine-learning notebooks use Spark to create or transform data. Task flow A visual workspace map that groups related Fabric items and shows how a user can move through the solution. It is a navigation aid, not proof that a process ran successfully. TMDL Tabular Model Definition Language, the text format used to define the Power BI semantic model in source control. Materialized view A continuously maintained query result stored by Eventhouse. It makes repeated summaries, such as sales by minute, faster to query.

items.title: Data-layer terms
items.text: Term Plain-language meaning Bronze The first data layer. It keeps source-shaped data with minimal changes. In this demo, optional Eventhouse shortcuts expose live event tables to Spark through the cusn schema. Silver The cleaned, typed, and consistently named data layer. This demo stores Silver tables in the ag schema. Gold The business-ready analytical layer. It contains summaries and model outputs designed for reporting or analysis. This demo stores Gold tables in the au schema. ag schema The short schema name used for Silver tables in this demo. For example, ag.fact_receipts contains durable receipt history. au schema The short schema name used for Gold tables and machine-learning outputs in this demo. For example, au.sales_minute_store contains summarized store sales. cusn schema The Lakehouse schema used for read-only shortcuts to Eventhouse tables. It lets Spark notebooks query live event data without copying it first. Medallion architecture Data organized into Bronze source records, Silver cleaned tables, and Gold summaries and model outputs. Shortcut A Fabric reference to data stored elsewhere. A shortcut makes data visible without creating another physical copy. Watermark A saved progress marker. ag._watermarks records how far a streaming transformation has processed so that the next run can continue safely.

items.title: Deployment and operations terms
items.text: Term Plain-language meaning Azure CLI Microsoft's command-line sign-in and management tool. The guided setup uses its signed-in identity to access the configured tenant. CI/CD Continuous integration and continuous delivery. In this repository, automated checks validate changes and deployment tooling publishes source-controlled Fabric items. Deployment profile A named package of demo capabilities. core is the smallest data-only profile, standard adds reporting and live-event assets, and full-demo adds preview and manually completed experiences. fabric-cicd Microsoft's open-source Python library for publishing source-controlled Fabric items into a workspace. Pipeline A repeatable sequence of activities. In this demo, pipelines run setup, transformations, and machine-learning notebooks in a controlled order. Preflight Checks performed before deployment changes Fabric. Preflight verifies configuration, sign-in context, capacity, tenant settings, and the intended target. REST API A web interface used by software to read or change Fabric resources. Deployment uses authenticated Fabric REST APIs for items, jobs, capacity checks, and readiness evidence. SKU or capacity tier The named size of a Fabric capacity, such as F64. The tier limits how much compute can run at one time. Terraform Infrastructure-as-code software used to create or resolve the workspace, Lakehouse, Eventhouse, capacity assignment, and related resources. Tenant The Microsoft Entra organization directory that owns identities, Fabric settings, capacities, and workspaces. Terminal success A run finished with a final Completed state. A successful request to start a pipeline is not terminal success because the work may still fail later. vCore Virtual processor core. Spark pool sizes and Fabric capacity limits are often expressed as vCores. SUCCEEDED Every selected required and optional readiness check passed. DEGRADED Required capabilities passed, but at least one optional capability has failed, stale, or missing evidence. The required demo path is usable; inspect the report before presenting the affected optional feature. FAILED A required capability failed or could not provide evidence. Do not present the deployment as ready. UNKNOWN The verifier could not obtain evidence for a selected check. A required UNKNOWN makes the overall result FAILED; an optional UNKNOWN makes it DEGRADED. SKIPPED The check does not apply to the selected deployment profile or verification mode. A skipped check does not count as a failure. IMP-* identifier A named improvement or implementation item in a technical backlog. The number provides a stable link to its acceptance criteria. ENH-* identifier An optional enhancement idea in a technical backlog. It is not required for the current supported demo unless another document says it has been implemented.

items.title: Streaming terms
items.text: Term Plain-language meaning Event A time-stamped message that describes something that happened, such as a receipt being created or inventory changing. Ingestion time When Eventhouse received an event. This can differ from the business event time because delivery is asynchronous. Micro-batch A small group of events processed together every few seconds. Grouping events makes streaming more efficient. Partition key A value used to keep related events together for processing. Consumers must still tolerate events arriving out of order. Spark Kusto connector The Fabric connector used by the Spark stream notebook to write event groups directly into Eventhouse KQL tables.

items.title: Machine-learning terms
items.text:
Term Plain-language meaning Model output A table containing a prediction, segment, forecast, or recommendation produced by a machine-learning notebook. Required model One of the six outputs needed by the Power BI report: demand forecast, customer segments, churn predictions, stockout risk, product recommendations, or price elasticity. Reporting is not published until these pass validation. Optional model An additional model that runs after Reporting in full-demo. Its failure does not remove the required report. Experimental model A preview output with stronger limitations. Treat it as an exploration, not an automated business decision.

The deployed walkthrough shows where these items appear in the workspace.

items.title: Operations guide
items.text:
Use this guide to check readiness, monitor data, and recover failures in an existing workspace. It is written for operators, analysts validating a demo, and support engineers. The plain-language glossary explains unfamiliar Fabric and data-layer terms.

See Deployment for provisioning and publication, the operations runbook for exact failure behavior, and the workspace inventory for selected assets and counts.

items.title: Readiness checklist
items.text:
Run the profile-aware live verifier after the selected workloads have run:

retail-setup verify --env <env>

This command is read-only. It resolves the selected profile and manifest, Terraform target outputs, and deployment journal, then writes an atomic, redacted report to:

deploy/.generated/<env>/readiness-report.json

The report provides one structured result for each target, item inventory, binding, KQL object group, schedule, pipeline, and freshness expectation. An unselected capability is SKIPPED; selected checks must produce evidence. Contributors can find the exact 26-row taxonomy in the operations runbook.

full-demo runs this taxonomy only after the ontology, both Data Agents, and the task flow have been published. The task-flow check compares the persisted workspace graph with the complete source graph, including every selected item reference and edge.

Result Meaning Exit SUCCEEDED Every selected check passed. 0 FAILED A required check failed or its evidence is unknown. 1 usage error The command or profile request is invalid. 2 DEGRADED Required checks passed, but optional evidence failed or is unknown. 3

DEGRADED means required scenarios are usable, but an optional feature is not ready to present. A new deployment where stream-events has not been started normally reports three optional unknowns:

  • no recent Silver streaming watermark;
  • no recent Eventhouse ingestion; and
  • no checkpoint identity attached to Eventhouse ingestion.

A recent watermark alone is not enough for a passing streaming check. The verifier also samples settled receipt/inventory keys and Gold sales against Silver, checking orphan keys and null balances. Missing or empty samples remain UNKNOWN; observed mismatches are FAIL. Both are optional streaming degradation. This bounded sample is not proof of every table or all historical data. See the sampling contract.

The report contains bounded counts, timestamps, the canonical manifest version/hash, resolved profile support and asset boundaries, target identities, and freshness lineage. It never stores access tokens, item-definition payloads, business rows, or raw service diagnostics.

Before running the verifier:

  1. Record the repository commit, environment, tenant, workspace, operator, and deployment run.
  2. Install utility/requirements-deploy.txt. On Windows and Linux it includes the bundled mssql-python driver; macOS requires Microsoft ODBC Driver 17 or 18. The verifier uses the existing Lakehouse SQL endpoint connection for setup, watermark, and model evidence.
  3. Confirm the configured identity can read Fabric items, definitions, job history, Eventhouse metadata, and the Lakehouse SQL endpoint.
  4. For core, which deploys no pipelines, run setup notebooks 01–11 manually in order before verification. Reporting profiles run setup 01–10 through setup-pipeline and setup-11-build-gold inside ml-required.
  5. For Reporting profiles, retain the deployment journal that correlates the exact setup and required-ML pipeline runs.
  6. Confirm optional ML, ontology, agent, dashboard, and rule features are ready before including them.
  7. Run a bounded stream before expecting streaming freshness checks to pass.

Use --run-pipeline only when you intentionally want the verifier to mutate the target by starting the profile's required post-publish pipeline:

retail-setup verify --env <env> --run-pipeline

The command waits for the exact returned job instance. It fails closed on an unknown state, timeout, mismatched run, or missing Location evidence. It does not start streaming, required ML, optional ML, or any schedule. A profile without a post-publish pipeline rejects this option as a usage error.

Different checks establish different facts:

Evidence What it proves Deploy command completed Required local subprocesses returned success. Artifact inventory passed Staged item count, folders, descriptions, and manifest/profile metadata match the selected publication phase. validate_deployment.py passed Generated config and staged files passed offline checks. Readiness report succeeded Required and optional selected live checks passed at the report timestamp. Readiness report degraded Required checks passed, but the deployment is not ready for the affected optional story. Pipeline trigger returned success Fabric accepted a run request; without exact-run terminal polling this is not completion. Pipeline/notebook run succeeded The selected activities completed in Fabric. Table row counts and timestamps advanced Data reached the expected serving layer. Report, ontology, or agent opened The surface exists; its binding and answer still need validation.

items.title: Monitor
items.text:
Use Fabric Monitoring Hub and item run histories for pipelines and notebooks. Use these signals together:

Signal What it tells you Where to check Historical setup run Whether the setup pipeline completed and setup-10 published the historical Silver snapshot (Gold is built by setup-11-build-gold) ag.setup_run_log in the Lakehouse Streaming progress How far the Eventhouse-to-Silver transform has processed ag._watermarks in the Lakehouse Live event freshness Whether Eventhouse is receiving recent events Eventhouse row counts and ingest_timestamp Gold freshness Whether business summaries reflect the latest selected inputs Representative maximum business time in au tables Machine-learning publication Whether a model output was generated by a known run Output generation time and model run identifier Alert state Whether optional detections or actions are pending The deployed alert or action table, when selected Deployment identity Which source revision and Fabric resources produced the evidence Git commit, deploy-run.json, and terraform-output.json

retail-setup verify checks these signals without saving source rows. For required machine learning, it checks the publication time and the identifier of the run that produced the same row. Business "as of" fields describe the source period; they do not prove when the model output was published. Setup and model evidence may be at most seven days old. Streaming watermarks, Eventhouse ingestion, and checkpoint evidence may be at most 30 minutes old. Pipeline and data timestamps must correlate with the retained deployment or explicitly triggered run.

items.title: Quick KQL checks
items.text:
KQL (Kusto Query Language) is Fabric's query language for Eventhouse. These queries are read-only examples.

Representative stream freshness (standard or full-demo):

receipt_created
| summarize rows = count(), latest = max(ingest_timestamp)

Representative event coverage:

union withsource=table_name receipt_created, payment_processed,
  inventory_updated, online_order_created
| summarize rows = count(), latest = max(ingest_timestamp) by table_name
| order by table_name asc

Truck lifecycle readiness:

fn_truck_sla()
| where arrival_ingest_timestamp > ago(30m)
| summarize rows = count(), latest = max(departure_ingest_timestamp),
    breaches = countif(dwell_minutes > 90)

Use table-specific event timestamps when a query depends on business time rather than ingestion time.

items.title: Common recovery paths
items.text: Symptom First action CLI tenant mismatch Reauthenticate to the configured tenant and rerun the dry-run target review. Capacity unavailable Confirm the capacity display name, active state, tenant, and operator access. Custom Spark pool provisioning fails Reconfigure with the starter pool unless preview support is intentional. Rendered notebooks missing Run retail-setup render --env <env>. Fabric publication fails Inspect the failing item type and generated deploy/.generated/<env>/fabric-cicd/parameter.yml. KQL objects missing Inspect and rerun the generated ordered database.kql against the intended database. Item inventory or notebook binding check fails Read the check's evidence in readiness-report.json for exact missing, duplicated, mismatched, or incorrectly bound items. Repair only the owning publication step; do not regenerate successful historical data. Notebook/report definition reads stall or lose their connection Each definition/export HTTP request has a 30-second timeout and bounded read-only retries. Once Fabric accepts the export, retries poll that exact operation rather than starting another export. Exhausted reads remain UNKNOWN, not successful evidence. Pipeline evidence reports ConnectionError Fabric collection reads retry connection resets and timeouts up to three times, within any collection deadline. If retries are exhausted, restore connectivity and rerun read-only readiness; do not rerun a successful pipeline just to recover its run evidence. Deployment exits because local pipeline monitoring timed out Keep the pipeline evidence file and run retail-setup deploy --env <env> --resume. Resume polls the exact recorded Location; it does not submit or cancel a Fabric run. Pipeline POST response was lost Do not retry manually until reconciliation finishes. The runner adopts only one recent exact-pipeline candidate in the request window; zero or multiple candidates fail closed and require an operator-supplied exact run ID. Late Fabric checks fail after a long verification run The Fabric REST session renews tokens within five minutes of expiry using the same configured credential and tenant. Renewal happens before sending a request, without replaying mutations or changing identities. If renewal fails, requests fail closed rather than sending an expired token. KQL readiness reports KustoNetworkError The read-only checker retries transient network errors. If retries are exhausted, restore Eventhouse connectivity and rerun readiness; this does not by itself indicate missing schema objects or require redeployment. Operations tables are missing after the native publisher failed Retry python -m deploy.scripts.deploy_operations_planning --environment <env> --operations-only when the environment excludes Planning. Missing tables are reported as FAIL with their names; the verifier does not query their mappings or discard otherwise readable KQL inventory. Operations source freshness validation fails The publisher retains its supporting tables and draft notebook, but does not seed invalid signals or create the agent. Inspect operations-planning-report.json; refresh the owning source/ML outputs before retrying monitoring publication. Do not bypass the seven-day freshness guard. retail-twins is missing after its publisher failed Retry python -m deploy.scripts.deploy_twins --environment <env>, then rerun read-only readiness. The selected twins report must exist and bind to the existing model; a non-blocking publisher failure is not evidence that this selected surface is ready. Setup pipeline not started Start setup-pipeline manually and retain its run ID. Setup pipeline failed Resume from the first failed activity only after validating upstream tables. Required ML gate failed Inspect producer/validator errors; Reporting is intentionally unpublished until a new exact run succeeds. Optional delivery training finds no valid completed dwell records Use the updated 13-ml-delivery-prediction notebook, which combines completed Silver fact_truck_moves with Bronze lifecycle events. Empty live shortcuts do not replace historical training data, and unmatched live arrivals remain prediction candidates. Republish the affected notebook and rerun only the failed optional pipeline; do not regenerate successful setup data. A failed optional pipeline hides successful sibling ML evidence Update the verifier and rerun read-only readiness. It correlates failed terminal runs as failures, verifies sibling pipelines independently, and checks each model's producer before querying its output. Missing producer evidence is not proof that the model SQL query or a sibling pipeline failed. freshness.setup_run_log reports ProgrammingError after deployment Update the local verifier to query setup data and staging catalog metadata separately, then rerun read-only readiness. Fabric error 15816 rejects a mixed catalog/data query; do not regenerate setup data for this checker error. Ontology, Data Agent, or task-flow links missing Run retail-setup post-ontology --env <env> to recreate any missing ontology, republish agents, and verify the exact persisted graph. Live rows absent Verify notebook parameters, resolved Query URI, KQL permissions, connector errors, and ingestion timestamps. Silver data stale Inspect Eventhouse shortcuts, transform run history, source timestamps, and ag._watermarks. Gold data stale Confirm the Silver run completed, then run the Gold transform. Power BI cannot see newly created tables Run python -m deploy.scripts.refresh_sql_endpoint --environment <env>, then reload the report and rerun readiness. Power BI shows the wrong workspace or data Confirm required tables exist and the Direct Lake binding targets the intended Lakehouse. Local validation passed but live assets fail Treat the deploy as not ready and perform item, binding, KQL, run, and data checks. Verifier reports UNKNOWN Restore the missing permission, locked dependency, output, journal, or live evidence; required unknowns are failures. Verifier reports stale evidence Run only the owning workload, retain its exact run evidence, and rerun the read-only verifier.

items.title: Negative stockout inventory at the required ML gate
items.text:
If notebook 15 rejects negative stockout_risk.current_inventory or days_of_inventory, update notebook 12's available-inventory calculation: known negative ledger balances represent zero available units, while unknown balances must still fail. Update notebook 15 for per-rule violation counts.

Republish the corrected notebooks and regenerate stockout_risk with 12-ml-stockout-prediction, then run 15-validate-required-ml-contract. Historical setup tables do not need regeneration for this derived-output repair. Reporting publication still requires a successful exact ml-required pipeline run; standalone notebook results do not replace that pipeline evidence. Do not weaken the gate or mark its failed run successful.

items.title: Rerun safely
items.text:
For a normal update:

  1. Preserve the failed or prior run identifiers.
  2. Confirm the target environment and workspace.
  3. Rerender notebooks when configuration or source changed.
  4. Preview the deployment plan.
  5. Deploy in place without recreate.
  6. Rerun only affected data workloads.
  7. Compare row counts, timestamps, and bindings with the prior known-good run.

Each workspace environment has isolated generation configuration, rendered output, Terraform state/data, and deploy/.generated/<env>/workspace/ staging, including post-ontology. Serialize runs for the same environment or Fabric target; local path isolation does not prevent concurrent remote writes.

items.title: Reset and recreate
items.text:
Use destructive operations only after:

  • validating the selected environment and live target;
  • retaining run, failure, and recovery evidence;
  • confirming which data and items will be removed;
  • receiving explicit operator confirmation.

retail-setup deploy --recreate destroys the workspace, exhausts paginated workspace listings until the target name is absent, and only then rebuilds it. A bounded timeout fails before apply.

99-reset-lakehouse is a manual destructive asset. It is not part of the normal pipeline.

items.title: Capacity
items.text: Runtime depends on store count, history months, Fabric capacity, Spark pool, notebook groups, and optional ML/ontology work. Begin with a bounded configuration and scale after observing Spark, Eventhouse, and Power BI utilization. Do not promise fixed runtimes without a measured profile.

items.title: Current live-stream boundary
items.text: The required historical, Reporting, ontology, Data Agent, and task-flow paths have live deployment evidence. The stream remains intentionally manual. Until a bounded stream-events run completes, the three optional streaming freshness checks remain UNKNOWN and overall readiness remains DEGRADED. This does not mean deployment failed. The console says Required deployment READY and presents missing initial stream evidence as informational rather than ERROR. There is no need to redeploy to clear that notice. Run the optional stream only when live-event functionality is needed; genuine stream failures and partial evidence still produce warnings.

items.title: Presenter journeys
items.text: Choose one of these 5-7 minute demonstrations for a specific audience. Each uses deployed Eventhouse tables and retail_querysets.KQLQueryset, without requiring a dashboard, ontology, or agent.

items.title: Common preflight and boundaries
items.text:
Before presenting:

  1. Complete Getting started, including the ordered KQL scripts and rendered stream-events.ipynb.

  2. Override the stream parameters with these presenter settings:

    source_rows_per_second = 10
sink = "eventhouse"
run_seconds = 180

The source template defaults to source_rows_per_second = 5 and run_seconds = 0; zero runs indefinitely. Each source row emits one scenario bundle, so the presenter settings create a three-minute bounded run rather than a fixed business-event count.

In Fabric, open the stream-events notebook, find the cell labeled Parameters, replace the values there, and then select Run all. Do not paste the values into a new cell; Fabric uses the designated Parameters cell when a notebook is started by automation. 3. Confirm the retail_querysets.KQLQueryset item is bound to that database. 4. Keep the Operations guide open for recovery.

After the notebook prints stopped after 180s, run the persona readiness query every 15 seconds for up to five minutes. Proceed only when every required row in that query has rows > 0 and a latest timestamp within the last 10 minutes. Eventhouse ingestion is asynchronous, so notebook completion alone is not readiness proof. For journeys that use mv_store_sales_minute, also run the store-sales query during that polling window and require at least one recent minute bucket.

These demonstrations exclude the following features:

  • Dashboard templates require validated import and binding (ENH-001).
  • Ontology and agent experiences require their capability, source, and access gates; the journeys do not depend on conversational answers.
  • Core journeys exclude ML. Reporting profiles fail closed on the required ML contract, and presenters must still confirm that the current model freshness check passes before discussing predictions.
  • Pricing actions and writeback remain optional (ENH-002).
  • Marketing attribution and return on ad spend (ROAS) are contract-tested but remain outside the core presenter path until a live Fabric journey is recorded.
  • Truck dwell is implemented but remains outside these core journeys until a bounded live run returns recent fn_truck_sla() rows.

items.title: Retail operations: live store and fulfillment pulse
items.text:
Show that store sales and fulfillment events are arriving, then investigate them by store or lifecycle stage.

Ask: "What is happening across stores and fulfillment right now, and what evidence shows that the feed is live?"

items.title: Assets and readiness
items.text:
Required source asset Readiness check Rendered utility/out/<env>/stream-events.ipynb from utility/notebooks/templates/driver-05-stream.py A bounded Eventhouse run completes without connector errors. Tables receipt_created, online_order_created, online_order_picked, and online_order_shipped from fabric/kql_database/01-create-tables.kql The preflight query below returns each table with a recent latest timestamp after streaming. Materialized view mv_store_sales_minute from fabric/kql_database/04-create-materialized-views.kql The sales query returns recent minute buckets. Queryset tab q_online_orders_15m from fabric/querysets/q_online_orders_15m.kql The tab opens against the intended KQL database.

Run this readiness check:

union withsource=table_name receipt_created, online_order_created,
  online_order_picked, online_order_shipped
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(10m)
| summarize rows = count(), latest = max(ingest_timestamp) by table_name
| order by table_name asc

items.title: Run the journey
items.text:
1. Introduce the question (30 seconds). Explain that these queries show recent events, not authoritative current state.

  2. Show store sales (2 minutes). Run:

    let lookback = 60m;
mv_store_sales_minute
| where ts > ago(lookback)
| project ts, store_id, total_sales, receipts, avg_basket
| order by ts desc

Expect recent minute buckets for one or more stores, with sales, receipt count, and average basket varying by store and time.

Say: "The stream writes typed receipt events to Eventhouse. This materialized view turns them into a bounded operational sales trend without waiting for a report refresh."

  1. Show fulfillment progression (2 minutes). Run:

    let window = 24h;
union withsource=stage online_order_created, online_order_picked,
  online_order_shipped
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(window)
| summarize events = count() by stage
| order by stage asc

Expect event counts for created, picked, and shipped stages. Counts need not match because the window is bounded and events can arrive out of order.

Say: "These are lifecycle event counts, not a claim that every order is currently in one stage. The shared order identifier supports deeper investigation when needed."

  1. Finish with freshness evidence (1 minute). Point to the latest ingestion timestamps. Add truck dwell only after a bounded live run returns recent paired lifecycle rows from fn_truck_sla() in the demo workspace.

items.title: Fallback
items.text:
• If the materialized view is empty, query recent receipt_created rows directly and show ingest_timestamp, store_id, and total.
  • If fulfillment stages are sparse, show q_online_orders_15m and describe order creation only.
  • If no live rows arrive, use the last successful bounded run and label its timestamp; do not substitute dashboard or truck-dwell claims.

items.title: Reset and recovery
items.text:
1. If the notebook exceeds its bounded run, cancel the active Spark query.
  2. Rerun it with source_rows_per_second = 10 and run_seconds = 180.
  3. Poll the readiness query every 15 seconds for up to five minutes; require all four tables and recent latest values.
  4. If they do not advance, verify the Query URI, database name, permissions, and notebook errors using Operations.
  5. Do not run the destructive Lakehouse reset for a presenter retry.

items.title: Merchandising: product demand and replenishment signals
items.text:
Identify products with recent sales, then compare their inventory, stockout-detection, and reorder signals.

Ask: "Which products are selling, and where should a merchandiser investigate replenishment signals?"

items.title: Assets and readiness
items.text:
Required source asset Readiness check Tables receipt_line_added, inventory_updated, stockout_detected, and reorder_triggered from fabric/kql_database/01-create-tables.kql The preflight query returns the available signal types and recent timestamps. Queryset tab q_top_products_by_sales from fabric/querysets/q_top_products_by_sales.kql The tab returns products with revenue and unit totals.

Run this readiness check:

union withsource=signal receipt_line_added, inventory_updated,
  stockout_detected, reorder_triggered
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(10m)
| summarize rows = count(), latest = max(ingest_timestamp) by signal
| order by signal asc

stockout_detected and reorder_triggered are conditional inventory events. If either row is absent after the first five-minute readiness wait, run one more bounded stream with the same presenter settings and repeat the wait. Present the replenishment step only after all four rows pass.

items.title: Run the journey
items.text:
1. Introduce the question (30 seconds). Explain that the demonstration combines demand and replenishment events without claiming a current inventory balance.

  2. Rank recent product demand (2 minutes). Open q_top_products_by_sales, or run:

    let window = 15m;
receipt_line_added
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(window)
| summarize revenue = sum(extended_price), units = sum(quantity)
    by product_id
| top 25 by revenue desc

Expect products to rank differently by revenue and units; the result uses product identifiers from typed receipt-line events.

Say: "This ranks recent demand by product. It is a starting point for investigation, not a forecast or recommendation."

  1. Inspect inventory movement (90 seconds). Run:

    let window = 30m;
inventory_updated
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(window)
| summarize movements = count(), net_quantity_delta = sum(quantity_delta),
    latest = max(ingest_timestamp)
    by store_id, product_id, reason
| top 25 by latest desc

Expect recent movement reasons and signed quantity changes for store/product combinations.

Say: "These are movements within the selected window. Summing deltas here does not reconstruct an authoritative on-hand balance."

  1. Show replenishment signals (90 seconds). Run:

    let window = 30m;
union withsource=signal stockout_detected, reorder_triggered
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(window)
| summarize events = count(), latest = max(ingest_timestamp)
    by signal, store_id, product_id
| top 25 by latest desc

Expect detection and reorder event types by store/product when generated in the selected window.

Say: "A detection or reorder is evidence that a workflow emitted a signal. We are not labeling the item as currently out of stock or the reorder as still pending."

  1. Finish with the limits (30 seconds). State what one row represents and what the metrics establish. Do not add marketing attribution, ML recommendations, or pricing writeback without their separate gates.

items.title: Fallback
items.text:
• Expand window to 24h after confirming older rows exist.
  • If inventory signals are absent, present the product-demand query and use the readiness result to explain which event types are missing.
  • If product detail is required but no validated dimension shortcut exists, keep product_id; do not invent names or categories.

items.title: Reset and recovery
items.text:
1. Rerun the bounded stream with source_rows_per_second = 10 and run_seconds = 180.
  2. Poll every 15 seconds for up to five minutes and require recent rows for receipt_line_added, inventory_updated, stockout_detected, and reorder_triggered.
  3. Because the last two events are conditional, run one additional identical bounded stream and repeat the poll before using the fallback.
  4. If a table is missing, reapply the ordered KQL scripts to the intended database; if rows are missing, follow the live-ingestion recovery path in Operations.
  5. Preserve prior events; no destructive reset is needed.

items.title: Executive and analytics: recent performance summary
items.text:
Summarize recent store sales, payment mix, and online-order volume. State the time window and what each row represents.

Ask: "What can leadership learn from the latest activity, and what evidence supports each headline?"

items.title: Assets and readiness
items.text:
Required source asset Readiness check Tables payment_processed and online_order_created from fabric/kql_database/01-create-tables.kql Each table returns a row count and latest ingestion timestamp. Materialized view mv_store_sales_minute from fabric/kql_database/04-create-materialized-views.kql Recent store/minute buckets are present. Queryset tabs q_tender_mix and q_online_orders_15m from fabric/querysets/ Both tabs run against the intended KQL database.

Run this readiness check:

union withsource=table_name payment_processed, online_order_created
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(10m)
| summarize rows = count(), latest = max(ingest_timestamp) by table_name
| order by table_name asc

items.title: Run the journey
items.text:
1. Introduce the summary (30 seconds). State that every result is synthetic, recent, and bounded by the query window.

  2. Show store performance (2 minutes). Run:

    let lookback = 60m;
mv_store_sales_minute
| where ts > ago(lookback)
| project ts, store_id, total_sales, receipts, avg_basket
| order by ts desc

Expect store/minute results with recent sales, transaction volume, and basket context without requiring a dashboard.

Say: "These rows show sales, receipts, and average basket by store and minute. Use the current results rather than numbers from an earlier demo."

  1. Show payment mix (90 seconds). Open q_tender_mix, or run:

    let window = 15m;
payment_processed
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(window)
| summarize amount = sum(amount) by payment_method
| order by amount desc

Expect payment methods to account for different shares of the recent processed amount.

Say: "This is payment-event mix for the selected window. It does not infer customer preference beyond the observed synthetic transactions."

  1. Show online demand (90 seconds). Open q_online_orders_15m, or run:

    let window = 15m;
online_order_created
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(window)
| summarize orders = count(), subtotal = sum(subtotal), tax = sum(tax),
    total = sum(total)
| extend aov = toreal(total) / toreal(orders)
| project orders, subtotal, tax, total, aov

Expect a summary of created-order count, value components, and average order value when rows are present.

Say: "This is created online demand, not completed revenue or a fulfillment service-level claim."

  1. Finish with the limits (30 seconds). State the source, time window, and grain. Use Power BI or a dashboard only if its binding and current data period were validated before the session. An unchecked agent answer is not a substitute for evidence.

items.title: Fallback
items.text:
• Expand the query window after confirming the most recent available timestamp.
  • If one channel has no recent rows, present the other supported queries and show the readiness result instead of manufacturing a complete scorecard.
  • Use direct KQL output if a report or dashboard binding is stale.

items.title: Reset and recovery
items.text:
1. Rerun the bounded stream with source_rows_per_second = 10 and run_seconds = 180.
  2. Poll the readiness query every 15 seconds for up to five minutes, then rerun the store-sales query and confirm recent minute buckets.
  3. If only the visualization fails, stay in the KQL queryset and follow the Power BI recovery entry in Operations.
  4. Do not clear Eventhouse or Lakehouse data between presentations.

Timing is a presentation target

The 5-7 minute duration describes the talk track, not deployment or data generation time. Measure setup and streaming on the selected Fabric capacity before scheduling a live session.

items.title: Sample retail questions: Data Agent & Ontology MCP
items.text:
Use these questions to evaluate the Fabric Data Agent over retail_model and Ontology MCP over the retail business graph. They are test prompts, not verified live answers. For a presentation, use the CIO walkthrough.

Retest each question with the current profile, identity, and data window. Some multi-hop ontology queries have failed. Avoid receipt_created sales-velocity queries, cross-entity event traversal, store N name resolution, and open-ended 360 views on the ontology. Prefer event counts grouped by store_id or dc_id, named-customer lookups, and relationships to ML predictions. Use the Data Agent or KQL for sales velocity.

items.title: Use case summary
items.text:
The demo models a synthetic retailer selling general merchandise and groceries through stores and online channels. Business users can ask about sales, inventory, customers, and operations without writing SQL, KQL, or DAX.

The Data Agent uses semantic-model measures for metrics, trends, and rankings. Ontology MCP exposes relationships among entities such as Store, Customer, Product, Receipt, and ChurnPrediction. The labels below identify the intended data source for each question; they do not guarantee that a service can answer.

Label Source Example content DA Data Agent over Lakehouse Silver/Gold through the semantic model Sales, margin, inventory, logistics, traffic, and marketing RT Eventhouse KQL event tables and materialized views Recent sales velocity, product sales, zone dwell, tender mix, and anomalies ONT Selected retail ontology graph Customer→Receipt→Product, Store←Truck←DC, Promotion→Customer; verify current bindings ML Predictive Gold tables Churn, segmentation, forecasts, stockout risk, market basket, elasticity, pricing, journeys, and delivery dwell

Start with sections 1-15 to test individual capabilities, then try the combined questions in section 16. Replace relative periods such as "last 30 days," "this quarter," and "yesterday" with dates present in your workspace.

items.title: 1. Executive & sales performance (DA)
items.text:
1. What were total net sales, gross profit, and gross margin % company-wide last quarter, and how did that compare to the prior quarter?
  2. Rank regions by net sales and units for the trailing 30 days, with each region's share of total sales.
  3. Which top 10 stores drove the most net sales last month, and how does each compare to the same month last year (YoY %)?
  4. Which store volume class (flagship, high_volume, standard, low_volume, kiosk) has the highest sales per store and average basket?
  5. What is total omnichannel revenue (in-store and online), and what percentage is digital? How has the channel mix changed since last year?
  6. Show month-over-month net sales trend for the last 6 months with the largest single-month swing called out.
  7. What are sales per customer and units per receipt company-wide, and which regions have above-average basket sizes?
  8. Which product departments have the largest sales gains and declines versus last year?

items.title: 2. Merchandising & product (DA / ONT)
items.text:
1. What are the top 15 products by revenue last month, and what is each product's gross margin %? (DA)
  2. For the Electronics department, show revenue and units by Category and Subcategory, drilling from Department → Category → Subcategory. (DA)
  3. Which products have the highest return volume? Are their returns spread across stores or concentrated in a few? (DA)
  4. Using the graph, list the distinct products a specific high-value customer has purchased through in-store receipts and online orders. (ONT)
  5. Through the ontology, find which stores sold a given product and which customers bought it. Show the Store → Receipt → Product → Customer path. (ONT)
  6. Which products have the highest MSRP-to-cost spread but the lowest sell-through? (DA)

items.title: 3. Omnichannel & fulfillment (DA)
items.text:
1. Compare average order value and units per order between in-store and online channels for the last 30 days.
  2. How is the fulfillment mix trending (Ship-from-DC vs Ship-from-Store vs BOPIS) month over month, and which mode is growing fastest?
  3. Which stores are absorbing the most Ship-from-Store and BOPIS volume, and is that concentrated in specific regions?
  4. What is online revenue year-to-date vs prior year, and what is the digital share of total omnichannel revenue?
  5. What is the payment tender mix (by method) and how does declined-payment rate vary by channel?

items.title: 4. Inventory, replenishment & supply chain (DA / ONT)
items.text:
1. What is current total units on hand across stores vs DCs, and the network inventory-to-sales ratio?
  2. Which stores have the most open high-priority reorders right now, and what is the total reorder fill gap?
  3. Rank DCs by units on hand and SKU count; which DC is carrying the most inventory relative to the stores it serves? (ONT)
  4. Through the graph, trace the replenishment path for a flagged store: which DC and which trucks service it (Store ← Truck ← DistributionCenter)? (ONT)
  5. What is average truck dwell time, and how many truck-dwell breach days occurred last month by site?
  6. Which stores show the highest stockout event counts, and does that correlate with their reorder fill gap?

items.title: 5. Stores, traffic & in-store experience (DA / RT)
items.text:
1. Which stores had the highest foot traffic but the lowest conversion (receipts per visitor) last week? (DA)
  2. What is average customer dwell time by store zone (Entrance, Electronics, Grocery, Clothing, Checkout), and where do customers stay longest? (DA)
  3. Show sales velocity (sales per minute) by store for the current hour. (RT)
  4. What were the top-selling products in the last 15 minutes across all stores? (RT)
  5. Which checkout zones have the longest dwell in the last few minutes, possibly indicating queues? (RT)

items.title: 6. Marketing & promotions (DA / ONT)
items.text:
1. What is total marketing spend and impressions by campaign last month, and the resulting CPM?
  2. Which promotions accounted for the most discount dollars, and how many receipts used each one? (DA)
  3. For a specific promo code, use the graph to find which stores ran it and which customers redeemed it (Promotion → Store / Promotion → Customer). (ONT)
  4. What is the promotion discount as a percentage of gross sales, and which department has the largest margin reduction from promotions?

items.title: 7. Customer segmentation (RFM, ML)
items.text:
1. How many customers fall into each segment (Champions, Loyal Customers, Potential Loyalists, New Customers, At Risk, Hibernating, Lost), and what is each segment's average lifetime value?
  2. What share of total monetary value comes from Champions and Loyal Customers, and how many customers does that represent?
  3. Which segment has gone longest since its last purchase, and what are its average purchase frequency and order value?
  4. Compare average order value across segments. Do Champions spend more per order, buy more often, or both?

items.title: 8. Churn prediction (ML / ONT)
items.text:
1. How many customers are predicted to churn, what is the predicted churn rate %, and what is the average churn probability across the base?
  2. List the high-risk customers (Risk Category = High) with the largest historical monetary value.
  3. Compare predicted and observed churn to check the model's precision and recall.
  4. Using the graph, show the RFM segment and recent purchase history of customers with the highest churn risk (Customer → ChurnPrediction + Customer → Segment). (ONT)
  5. Which region or store has the highest concentration of high-risk, high-value customers?

items.title: 9. Demand forecasting (ML)
items.text:
1. What are total forecasted units for the next horizon by store, and which stores have the widest confidence interval (most uncertain demand)?
  2. Which product/store combinations have the highest forecast mean absolute percentage error (MAPE)?
  3. For a given high-volume store, show forecasted units vs lower/upper bound for its top products.
  4. Where does forecasted demand most exceed current on-hand inventory, suggesting a need for replenishment?

items.title: 10. Stockout risk (ML / ONT)
items.text:
1. Which store/product positions are at high stockout risk, ranked by stockout probability, and how many days of inventory remain?
  2. How many SKUs are flagged high-risk, and what is the average days-of-inventory and daily demand velocity across them?
  3. Compare stockout-risk predictions with open reorders. Which high-risk SKUs lack a pending reorder? (ONT)
  4. For the highest-velocity products, which stores have the thinnest cover (lowest days of inventory)?

items.title: 11. Market basket / recommendations (ML)
items.text:
1. Which product pairs have the highest association lift and confidence, making them candidates for cross-merchandising or bundling?
  2. For a given anchor product, what are the top recommended add-on products and the confidence of each association?
  3. Which high-lift product associations cross department boundaries, such as a grocery item associated with an electronics accessory?

items.title: 12. Price elasticity & dynamic pricing (ML)
items.text:
1. Which products are Highly Elastic versus Inelastic, and what do those estimates suggest about price sensitivity?
  2. Show the dynamic-pricing recommendations with the largest gap between current price and elasticity-optimal price, with the model's confidence on each.
  3. For elastic products, what revenue lift does the recommended price imply, and which constraints are binding?
  4. Which categories are most price-sensitive, and what does that suggest for promotion planning?

items.title: 13. Customer journey & behavior (ML / RT)
items.text:
1. What are the most common in-store zone-transition paths, and where do journeys most often end without reaching Checkout (drop-off)?
  2. Which zones have the highest dwell, and where do customer journeys most often end?
  3. Which customers (by BLE id) have moved through at least three zones in the current live session without a purchase? (RT)

items.title: 14. Delivery / logistics prediction (ML)
items.text:
1. What are the predicted truck-unload dwell times and prediction intervals for upcoming deliveries? Which sites are at risk of long dwell?
  2. Which lanes or sites consistently exceed predicted dwell, suggesting a structural bottleneck?

items.title: 15. Real-time anomaly detection (RT)
items.text:
1. Are there any sales or inventory anomalies detected in the last hour (sudden velocity spikes/drops)?
  2. Which stores are showing abnormal stockout-detection or reorder-trigger rates right now versus their normal baseline?

items.title: 16. Combined metrics, relationships, and predictions
items.text:
These questions require multiple data sources or model outputs. Treat them as evaluation targets, not as a supported sequence of autonomous actions.

  1. Identify Champions and Loyal customers flagged as high churn risk, list their preferred departments, and suggest products for a win-back offer using segments, churn predictions, purchase history, and market-basket associations. (ONT, ML)
  2. What is the total historical revenue associated with high-churn-risk customers? Keep historical spend separate from estimates of future revenue at risk. (DA, ML)
  3. For products at high stockout risk in high-traffic stores, estimate at-risk daily sales using forecasted demand velocity. (ML)
  4. For the top 10 promoted products with the largest margin reductions, compare price elasticity. Which discounts applied to products estimated to be inelastic? (DA, ML)
  5. Where does next-period forecasted demand exceed combined store and DC inventory, and is a truck already scheduled for that store? (ML, ONT)
  6. Compare zone dwell and store conversion. Do stores with longer Checkout dwell have lower conversion? (ML, DA)
  7. For each store with sales below its regional median, list its top stockout risk, churn-risk customers, and recommended cross-sell in priority order. (DA, ONT, ML)

items.title: Notes for the tester
items.text:
ML questions in sections 7-14 and 16 require predictive Gold tables. The ml-required pipeline gates six outputs: churn_predictions, customer_segments, demand_forecast, stockout_risk, product_recommendations, and price_elasticity. Post-Reporting ml-optional produces journey_patterns and dwell_predictions; ml-experimental produces pricing_recommendations. Confirm the relevant pipelines ran and their tables are populated and bound before testing.

Real-time questions require fresh Eventhouse event tables and materialized views. Run the streaming notebook and check ingestion freshness first.

items.title: Workspace and profile inventory
items.text:
Use this guide for exact profile contents and item counts. For an overview of what the demo does, start with Use cases or the plain-language glossary.

contracts/retail-demo.json defines stable IDs, descriptions, support status, source pointers, profiles, boundaries, prerequisites, commands, paths, ML tiers, publication expectations, and readiness taxonomy. It is currently manifest version 1.4.0.

Physical fields, tables, notebook bodies, pipeline bodies, and the Tabular Model Definition Language (TMDL) files for Power BI remain in their authoritative sources. Contract tests derive inventories from those sources and check the counts in this guide.

items.title: Canonical commands
items.text:
python scripts/setup.py
retail-setup configure --workspace-name retail-demo-dev
retail-setup render --env dev
retail-setup deploy --env dev --dry-run
retail-setup verify --env dev

Every entry point, including direct scripts/setup.py and retail-setup commands, defaults to the manifest-default full-demo profile. Render, deploy, and verify resolve the stored profile from the --env environment.

items.title: Deployment profiles
items.text:
Profile Support Logical assets Groups Pipelines KQL scripts Infrastructure Reporting Total core core/explicit 1 1 0 0 12 0 12 standard supported/explicit 8 4 5 6 37 2 39 full-demo preview/default 14 8 7 6 47 2 49

The logical asset selections are:

  • core: asset.lakehouse.
  • standard: asset.lakehouse, asset.eventhouse, asset.stream-events, asset.data-pipelines, asset.kql-queryset, asset.ml-notebooks, asset.semantic-model, and asset.report.
  • full-demo: all standard assets plus asset.dashboard-templates, asset.activator-rules, asset.task-flow, asset.ontology, asset.data-agents, and asset.custom-spark-pool.

core uses only core assets. standard adds optional assets but no preview assets. full-demo adds preview task-flow, ontology, Data Agent, and custom-pool assets. Dashboard templates and Activator rule definitions are reference source files, not items published by deployment. No profile selects the destructive reset group, starts the long-running stream, or enables a schedule.

The Reporting profiles publish infrastructure first, wait for setup and the required ML validator to reach terminal success, then publish Reporting. full-demo runs optional and experimental ML only after Reporting. Ontology creation, both Data Agents, and exact task-flow publication then complete automatically in the same deployment. The two Data Agents are counted in their separate post-ontology publication phase rather than the initial infrastructure count.

items.title: Workspace folders and publication phases
items.text:
Profile Infrastructure folders Reporting folders Root-level staged items core Notebooks, Lakehouses none none standard Notebooks, Lakehouses, KQL Querysets, ML Experiments, Pipelines Reports, Semantic Models none full-demo Notebooks, Lakehouses, KQL Querysets, ML Experiments, Pipelines Reports, Semantic Models; then automatically completed Data Agents none

Eventhouse and its default KQL database are Terraform-owned and are therefore not duplicated as staged shell items. Every staged .platform description is validated against the selected manifest asset description. Deployment writes a phase-specific artifact-inventory-<phase>.json beside the environment state; it records the profile, manifest version/hash, expected and actual counts, folders, and core/optional/preview/manual boundaries.

The final organization step also places native/optional items in object-type folders such as Eventhouses, Ontologies, and Fabric Apps. Service-managed children remain with their parents. See the folder mapping.

items.title: Data, event, and model inventory
items.text:
The source defines these counts:

  • Historical Lakehouse: 36 tables, comprising 7 dimensions, 19 facts, and 10 Gold aggregates.
  • Live events: 18 emitted business event types and 19 KQL event tables. The extra table, unknown_event, is a non-emitted operational catch-all.
  • Active Direct Lake semantic model: 42 tables, comprising the 36 historical tables and 6 required ML outputs.
  • Data/event registry: 3 data contracts, 19 declared paths, and 4 intentional exceptions.

For exact table and event definitions, see the historical data contract, live event contract, and Power BI semantic model specification.

items.title: ML tiers
items.text:
Tier Contracts Publication behavior required 6 Must pass the runtime contract validator before Reporting publishes. optional 5 Runs after Reporting only in full-demo; failure degrades, not blocks, required Reporting. experimental 3 Runs after Reporting only in full-demo; preview limitations apply.

The six active Reporting tables are demand forecast, customer segments, churn predictions, stockout risk, product recommendations, and price elasticity. Optional and experimental outputs are not silently added to the 42-table semantic model.

items.title: Readiness contract
items.text:
The readiness report covers:

  • the intended workspace and resource IDs;
  • the selected item inventory;
  • notebook, pipeline, Power BI, queryset, Data Agent, and task-flow bindings;
  • KQL tables, functions, mappings, and materialized views;
  • schedules and exact pipeline-run results; and
  • setup, streaming, machine-learning, and alert freshness.

Required checks protect the supported historical and Reporting paths. Optional checks cover manually started streaming and preview/extended experiences. This is why a usable workspace can report DEGRADED when the optional stream has not been started. Contributors can find the exact 26 check IDs in the operations runbook.

Dry-run output, the deployment journal, artifact inventories, and readiness reports all expose the resolved profile and canonical manifest version/hash. Live execution evidence remains environment-specific; consult Operations for exit codes and live-only gates.
